utterances.text: Okay. Orientation. My apartment is to the south or south-west from Fontana. It is at the crossroads in the centre of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that night, that afternoon and that night of 13 July that you spent the night there, this Court has heard evidence that there were many, many buses and trucks full of Muslim men parked in lines throughout the town of Bratunac, some in front of the Vuk Karadzic school complex, some in front of Vihor, some in front of the brigade command, and that there were literally thousands of Muslim men of military age that were in the town that night. Does this help your recollection at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it. I heard this from people and from my sons, that things of this kind were happening. But however, when one carries out such activities during the day for a whole day, one gets tired, one has to go to bed. I didn't see this. I didn't watch this. I had no reason to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, these vehicles, these buses, these trucks, it is the position of the Prosecution that those are the same buses and trucks that were used to move the population out of Potocari, some of those same buses and trucks that were filled up from fuel that was organised by you and others. And that on the morning of the 14th July, some convoy, at least a kilometre, a kilometre and a half long, with all those thousands of Muslims in it, took off towards Zvornik. All those buses and trucks needed a lot of very expensive, very valuable fuel. They would have been filled up probably at the Vihor garage, at the Bratunac Brigade fuel station that we've heard about, and the logistics officer might have heard about this in some respect. Can you tell us anything about this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have a single document to the effect that the fuel was taken on the 14th. I do have such documentation for the 13th, but not the 14th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you can't tell us a thing about it from your memory?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the thousands of Muslims in that convoy --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Your Honour. This is irrelevant, what happened to them. He answered: I didn't see it, I didn't watch it, I had no reason to. He was asked about the fueling, and he said nothing, that he didn't know anything about it. Now he wants to go into this line about what happened to these people. What is the relevance with respect to this particular witness and his involvement? This is nothing but prejudicial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, the witness himself is from Bratunac, and I believe that -- I haven't seen the follow-up questions yet, but I believe that Mr. Karnavas [sic] will ask about the destination of this witness, whether -- the destination of those victims, whether this witness knows or not. It's a reasonable question. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that these thousands of Muslims were taken up to the Zvornik area and murdered?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this later and I read about it in the papers and it was also reported on television. But at the time I didn't know because we, the members of the brigade, did not take part in it. We had no say as to where they would be transported to. Mladic said they would be taken in the direction of Tuzla, whether that was to be via Kladanj or Zvornik, I didn't know. And I had no idea who would be making the decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the Bratunac Brigade military police led the convoy that took these people to their deaths? Two members of the Bratunac military police were at the Pilica school when a busload of Muslims were shot and killed with automatic weapons. You never heard anything about any of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have no idea where the fuel came from that went into all these buses and trucks or who put them in there that morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Asked and answered, first of all. And second of all, the Prosecutor now is testifying. Where is there evidence that any fuel was being put in those buses on the morning of the 14th? It's just a pure assumption. I can understand the gentleman is angry after seven years of working on the case, but we've gone far enough on this line of questioning. Where is the proof that on the morning of the 14th buses were actually fueled? If he has it, he can show it to the gentleman. They could have been fueled on the 12th, they could have been fueled on the 13th. Obviously, they needed fueling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I can respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First of all, asked and answered is not a proper objection on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I beg to differ on this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it can be, if it gets to the point where it's argumentative and the question is not needed to be asked, but on cross-examination to make a point or to test a witness, it is perfectly appropriate to ask a question again. And unless I say it crosses the line where we've all had enough, then it's perfectly appropriate. It's not a proper objection. Secondly, I don't think there's anything wrong with that question. I mean, these buses had to have had fuel. And we know from the facts of the case all the work they were doing on the 12th and 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think to save time there's no need to repeat the same question again and again. I think both parties have to be aware of that. And secondly, I believe that the witness already answered that question, unless you make some differences with previous questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever get any information that the fuel records for this -- for the 14th were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection to this. It assumes that they were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, during the cross-examination the party who is conducting the cross-examination could ask any questions that are possible. We have the witness here. He could answer that question by himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, perhaps Mr. Karnavas has forgotten, but we do have a long list of documents that were, in fact, destroyed. And I don't know what's on it, but I know it's been proven in this case that documents were destroyed, so it's a perfectly reasonable question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about documents, fuel documents, getting destroyed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we never destroyed any documents about refueling or fuel, or we never destroyed any documents on any materiel or equipment. I never got any such orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't know anything about the reburial of over a thousand people from Glogova to Zeleni Jadar and other places in September and October 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, I did hear about those activities, but I assert that the Bratunac Brigade neither provided security for -- neither provided the transportation means nor the fuel for those activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do know about it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was said here yesterday that Nikolic reported -- informed the command that he had undertaken those activities according to orders from the VRS Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until that point, until the day when he informed us. Namely, I didn't know why the operation was going on. I wasn't aware of it. I only found out about it after Captain Nikolic had informed us about it at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're now telling us that this meeting in October that's in the meeting minutes where "asanacija" is referred to was in fact a reburial of the bodies operation, as far as you know.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Nikolic did not give us any explanations, and we didn't ask him to clarify anything; why or what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go back to your interview again. And this is page 51, line 5. It's -- for you, it's page 49, line 1. And Mr. Manning says: "As you said before, the buses and trucks are being organised. The fuel is being organised from UNPROFOR, and there's a large amount happening that day. There must be something that sticks in your head --"

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. Page 49, line -- which line?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Try line 1, around line 1.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see it. All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. "There must be something that sticks in your head. When you went back to your headquarters, did you explain to Blagojevic what you had done in relation to the trucks and buses? Did you explain about the 30.000 litres of fuel from UNPROFOR? Did he give you another task?" And you: "I would rather inform about the buses and trucks and the fuel the colonel in the rear service than Blagojevic himself." Mr. Manning says: "And why is that?" And you say: "We were just one unit under corps command, which was in command of the operation, and the collection of buses and everything was done by the corps."

utterances.speaker: MR. MANNING
utterances.text: "So therefore you would report back to the corps." And you say: "That's logical, and I must have done it like that. "Wouldn't you have also had to advise your commander, particularly as you were using his resources?" And you say: "Of course. After everyone else, then commander, too. But the transportation itself we didn't organisation." Do you stand by that statement today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we just go -- continue on a little bit on the same page. You also state -- you were also asked: "Of course" -- no, you say -- "Wouldn't you also have to advise the commander?" You say: "Yes." You say: "Of course. After everything, then the commander, but the transportation itself we didn't organise." Then the next question is: "You provided the equipment and the fuel and the driver." And your answer is: "Part of the vehicles that we had in our possession. What we had on our disposal we put on disposal to the corps." You stated that. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me go back to the issue of mobilisation, because I think it's an important concept. Can you go to Vihor and just simply take vehicles from them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this situation I knew that the mobilisation was being done by the corps, so that there was no need for me to engage those buses myself because the corps had already done it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But generally speaking, when you want to mobilise a bus from Vihor, can you just show up there, announce yourself, and just take the vehicle? Or is there a particular process that you would have to go through?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, there was a procedure to be observed, a process to be observed. In some instances, we would do it on an internal, so to speak, basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Aleksandar Tesic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's his position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in charge of a section of a department in the Ministry of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he would be involved in a process of mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is going beyond the scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well within.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're not contesting the mobilisation --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It sounded to me like he was. It sounded to me like the suggestion was that he could just go there and take and use as he pleased.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's what he said. He just said again sometimes they could go and do things. We know the mobilisation process. He suggested that the corps had already done it. Going back to Mr. Tesic and the entire RS mobilisation process is beyond the scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: With that concession, Your Honour, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked a question about being -- about the commander being well-informed. Do you recall that, early on, about how the commander was always being well-informed? This was --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to show you a part of your statement. It's on page 35 for us, line 10. And it would be line 34 for you, line 34 -- I mean page 34, line 34. And you're being asked a question by Mr. Vlasic, a Mark Vlasic. And the question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's not proper on direct to just read to your witness. You can provide it to the witness to refresh his recollection and ask him about the subject; you can use it to impeach. But you can't just go reading the statement and asking questions. That's improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First of all, I'm entitled to rehabilitate the witness. This is a form of rehabilitation. What the Prosecution has done in their cross-examination is show that everybody reports to Blagojevic and Blagojevic is kept well-informed. Here he's asked concretely about Momir Nikolic, and the gentleman stated contrary with respect to Nikolic. And yesterday, you will note, that I brought out the fact that the gentleman had worked in the security sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, you draw the attention of this witness to certain lines and at certain pages, then you ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If you are not satisfied with that answer, you might read that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 34, line 34. And please review that section with respect to your answer on Momir Nikolic and his reporting habits as a member of the security organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What is the -- what's the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 35. Page 35, line 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right around that section, and if you go further down -- line 15 is the answer that would guide us to the rehabilitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My questions were directed towards this witness and -- well, I will sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see your answer with respect to the security organ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 34, line 34?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you read downwards -- if you read the next few lines with respect to Nikolic reporting to Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was led into a situation here. I have been in a situation here to say that this was from the 12th, but this was not indeed something which happened from the 12th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you -- now, this is why I need to read from the document. Do you recall being asked the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would like to have the rules --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll hear him out, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The rules we worked by in the Prosecution's case: If refreshing the recollection doesn't help, then he -- if the witness can be declared hostile then he can be declared hostile and he can be asked leading questions. This is the rule we worked under. And I'm certainly willing to break the rules to get finished, but you break the rule once and you break the rule a thousand times, and it adds up. And I just want to point out that is the rule we all know we worked under, and that is the rule Mr. Karnavas was trained in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes, I agree with you generally in the rules. But here it seems to me that I could not understand the answer by this witness. So in this situation, I believe there is a necessity for the Defence counsel to take a lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall being asked: "So therefore Nikolic will report to Blagojevic as to what's happening, what he's been ordered to do, if in fact he was taking orders from the corps security organ?" And do you recall giving this answer: "Security organs always work separately from others. There's always some kind of secrecy around them." Do you recall giving that answer? That's your answer. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then he goes on: "But surely there's some contact of reporting from Blagojevic and Nikolic while they're there at the same time?" And your answer is: "It's possible." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you said yesterday -- or when you said to the Prosecution when they were being -- you were being questioned there about secrecy around the security organ, could you please explain to us what you meant, in light of the fact that you were working for the security organ at some point in time prior to becoming the assistant commander for rear services.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organs always cooperated with the superior command. That means that was the principle of the work which obtained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you were asked a series of questions about your answer with respect to Colonel Blagojevic being in Potocari. I want to direct your attention to line -- to page 9, and if you could read to yourself from page 9 line 4, read that page, a portion of it. And please tell us whether you concretely say that the commander was indeed there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say concretely that it was so; I supposed that he could be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what -- could you please tell us exactly what you told the Prosecutors back then, so at least we have a flavour as to how you put it. And this is line 9. This is early on in the interview for what is going to take place over the course of nine hours. Please read to us how exactly you put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, do we have to go into those details? I think everything we get is already there. The witness said that, you know, he was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. And -- but I want to make sure that the record is clear, because the gentleman here is saying we must have, probably, supposedly. This is throughout the whole transcript. Now, I could forego my entire line of re-direct if I was assured that this entire statement could enter into evidence, and therefore I could point out and plug holes into the Prosecution's theory that Colonel Blagojevic was in Potocari as a result of this gentleman's testimony. Unless the Prosecution now wishes to concede, as I believe Mr. Butler conceded, that Colonel Blagojevic was not in Potocari on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this man testified under oath yesterday that he told the Prosecutor that Blagojevic was not in Potocari. He didn't say he hemmed or he hawed or it was a maybe or probably. He told this court yesterday that he told us that he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, that's wrong, contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas had plenty of chance to use this on direct and he didn't use it and we're just going over and over it again. I think it's clear what's happened here. I think the Court understands it. I don't have any objection to this whole document coming in, if you can stand another document. I have no problem. Maybe that can solve our problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour. I think Mr. McCloskey might be mistaken. The gentleman said that he told the Prosecutors that Blagojevic was there on the 12th, but he was wrong in stating that. He never denied that he didn't tell the Prosecutors that Blagojevic was there on the 12th. I think maybe we're all tired and maybe it was Monday, but I distinctly remember the gentleman stating that, yes, he told the Prosecutors that -- in Banja Luka on the 26th of November that Blagojevic was there, and now he's saying: I was wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, so there's no dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So there's no disputes on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I also want to point out that the whole statement itself is full of maybes, probablies, I suppose, which shows that he's trying -- it fits well into the gentleman's testimony that he's trying to provide answers and he's guessing half the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So can we have the whole document admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's a difficult question; we'll deal with it at a later stage. But I don't think on this particular issue that there's any dispute on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked about the 5th Engineering Company at Konjevic Polje. Do you know what they were doing there? Who ordered them there and what was their function -- the 5th Engineer's Battalion. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you were asked a series of questions by the Prosecutor about the 5th Engineer's Battalion that were in Konjevic Polje back in 1994, I believe, is when they arrived. But do you know who brought them there and what was their function? Why were they there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say with certainty. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Colonel Blagojevic had anything to do with them being there? Concretely now.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just one other question. You were asked a series of questions about the separation of the men. I want you to look at, in the English version page 30, and if we can start on line 14. On the Srpski version -- just a second. It would be page 30, right around line 15. If you could read all the way down. There are a couple of lengthy questions, and some information is provided to you regarding what was happening in the Krstic case, by Dean Manning. Could you read that, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell us: Were you asked during your interview in Banja Luka about whether you saw any separation of men there while you were in Potocari? Do you recall being asked that question?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, in part of the questioning process, Dean Manning even provided you with some information from the Court in the Krstic case. Right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV TRISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time when you were asked that question -- those questions, did you not tell him that while you were there you did not see any separation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm trying to adjust to these new rules, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a leading question which is not allowed on direct examination --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no idea where these rules are being made up. I would like to have -- Seriously, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This is a re-direct. I think in the re-direct you could ask leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is not my understanding. If that is a rule coming from the Bench, I will gladly follow it, but re-direct is normally the same as direct, especially when I am limited to no re-cross. We have to be very careful not to allow leading questions or allow him to go beyond the scope. You don't argue your case through direct, which is what he's doing. That is completely improper; it's happening to each one of these witnesses. It's relatively harmless in this case, I'll grant it, but what I'm trying to do is prevent this constant slippage into this kind of conduct because it will go on and on and on. Leading questions in re-direct, generally not accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as I said before that the re-direct examination should be strictly within the cross-examination. And since all the matters have already been raised in the direct examination and the cross-examination, there is some leverage in the re-direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This does not mean that we'll provide you the opportunity to conduct your direct examination once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I totally understand, Your Honour. And frankly, I'm at a loss at some of the things that I'm hearing from the Prosecutor. I will try to re-organise my thoughts to comport with, perhaps, this new method of trial advocacy. But frankly, I don't know what he's talking about. But in any event, I have no more questions at this stage. I'm through with my re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's time for a break. Should we -- well, since the Judges have no questions, I think we will continue with the admission of the evidence so to finish this witness before the recess. At this stage, are there any documents to tender? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I believe it's -- I believe it's D155, which was the -- it's dated 28 June, 1995 -- actually, maybe we don't need to have to admitted since we already found that it was not relevant to the events surrounding Srebrenica, so I withdraw that. The series of documents under D166, that would be 1 through 10, those were the materiel lists dated 5th July 1995 to 12 July 1995. D156, which is an overview of the amounts of fuel, lubricants, et cetera, received and consumed between 1 July 1995, and 31 July 1995. It's dated 2 August, 1995. D157, the materiel lists of 12 July 1995. D158, the materiel lists which is 13 July 1995. D159, which is a receipt with respect to the UNHCR fuel, that's dated 14 July 1995. D160, the handwritten document of 12 July 1995. D161, handwritten document; this is the listing of fuel for 12 July 1995. D152, handwritten document again. D163 -- it should be D162 and then 163, the appropriation of equipment from the former enclave, dated 24 July 1995. D164, which is the intelligence -- it's a document from the intelligence sector dated 13 July 1995; that was from Colonel Jankovic. And D165, which I'm sure the Prosecution has no objections to, which are the Bratunac Brigade minutes of the meeting of 28 June 1965 to 16 October 1965. I believe that's it. Now, I should -- and then, of course, the statement, which should come in as D167 -- 171, I'm sorry. 171. And I should note that some of the documents we have unofficial translations, though they are before the registrar to be formally translated. And I would suspect since we've already done most of the work for them, it's just a matter of perhaps fine tuning and giving it the registrar's imprimatur as official translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just one second, if I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any documents to tender on your part?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me one second. Thank you for your patience. We have two documents that have been mentioned here. One is the document that -- of October 1993, mentioning that Lieutenant Colonel Blagojevic was assigned as chief of staff of the Bratunac Brigade. And the other is the copy of the preparatory order dated 2 July, number one, that was referred to in another document. Just to clear the record, and I see Mr. Karnavas -- we understand each other on that. Unfortunately, the copy was not readable for the witness, but it's a military preparatory order for the attack. And I don't think there's any problem. I think it's a historic document the Court should have as other key documents referred to it. And just to remind the Court, both these documents are important documents that were referenced in Rick Butler's report, and we offered into evidence before but they were declined. So that's why they have not been offered into evidence before. And I will try to find more documents like this so -- because I think it's important that the Court, in order to understand Mr. Butler's report, has those documents, because many of them are significant. As you know, I didn't want to go over every document cited by Mr. Butler, otherwise, he would still be on direct examination. But if there are any other key documents, I will try to find some time and bring those up. A few pop up from witnesses, so we bring them up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, would you please furnish us with the number of those two documents you offered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The re-assignment is P857, that's the document dated 2 October. And the preparatory order dated 2 July is P862.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So these documents tendered by the Defence counsel as well as by the Prosecution are admitted into the evidence. As for the document D171, which is the statement of this witness, as a rule we do not admit the previous statement into the evidence. But since the Defence counsel tendered this document and there's no objections from the Prosecution on this very document, this document is admitted into evidence. But, however, there must be a rule to solve the conflict between the live testimony and this statement. If in the future there is any conflict, the live testimony of this witness should have the primacy. It is so decided. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. When this sitting is adjourned, the usher will show you out of the room. We wish you a pleasant journey back home. The hearing is adjourned and we will resume at quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Karnavas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zlatan Celanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your last name letter by letter.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: C-e-l-a-n-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are you from, Mr. Celanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: In Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you currently do in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I have my own private business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a lawyer, and I have an agency for real estate and legal assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long have you been a lawyer, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Since 1980.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just briefly, could you tell us, where did you study, where did you get your law degree from?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I studied in Belgrade, and that's where I got my law degree from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in 1992 were you mobilised when Bratunac had the Territorial Defence there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us what position you held when you were mobilised with the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Are you referring to the army or before I was mobilised? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No problem. Before the formation of the Bratunac Brigade, we know, we've heard testimony, that there was a Territorial Defence, a TO, in the Bratunac municipality. Were you a member of the TO prior to the formation of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us first of all when it was that you became a member of the TO.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: 16 April 1992 I was mobilised by the military department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And could you please tell us, what position or what function did you have with the TO when you were mobilised back on 16 April 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: At first I was a foot soldier, a military policeman since I was mobilised into the military police company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other functions did you hold?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I don't understand your question, sir. What functions I had in addition to being a foot soldier or what I did? Can you clarify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What else did you do, if anything, besides being a foot soldier when you were with the TO?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand. I was involved in legal affairs. I was an official in charge of legal affairs, religious affairs, and moral guidance. This was my professional duty at the level of the desk officer. Do you want me to go into any other detail?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That will be fine for now. When the Bratunac Brigade was formed in 1993, do you recall what position you held with them? When you first got -- became a member of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you an assistant commander for legal, religious, and moral guidance?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you in that position?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Until the day of mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Until the day of demobilisation or the day -- mobilisation. Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Demobilisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what -- so what year -- what month and year would that be?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe it was sometime before the Dayton, a few days before the Dayton accords were signed in 1995, in the month of December of that year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, first I want to talk about -- let me direct your attention to July 1995. Could you please tell us, what position did you hold within the Bratunac Brigade then?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: The one I described. I was the desk officer for legal affairs, religious affairs, and moral guidance in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Could you please tell us what your functions were in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: My main tasks were to deal with breaches of military discipline committed by army members and to participate in any procedure against those who would commit a breach of discipline or break rules against the army, in keeping with the law. My duty was to, in such cases, if such a person was brought in by the military police on the order of the superior officer, I would take a statement from such a person about the circumstances under which the breach of law took place. Sometimes I would also hear eyewitnesses of the event. I would also be in charge of maybe obtaining a written document about the event. After that, my duty was to inform the brigade commander, or previously the battalion commander, about the incidents, what kind of an incident it was. If my opinion was sought, then I would qualify the incident, either as a misdemeanor or a crime, and what should be done. This was more or less what I did within the scope of my duties. In addition to that, I had some other duties. One of those involved occasional controls of the UNHCR convoys that were transporting food to Srebrenica. I would be checking whether there were any weapons hidden among the food. And this was basically what I did. I would escort those convoys in order to inspect them. In addition to that, I was also in charge of taking statements, even from civilians brought in by the army, because sometimes civilians also did something that damaged the army or something that was targeted against the army. They would sometimes use arms against the law or they would do other things, and one of my tasks was to conduct interviews with prisoners of war. Should those be brought in, I would take a statement for -- from such a person. I would write my report based on that statement and forward that to my commander. I would inform my commander what I had heard during the interview with such a person. The essence of that job was to establish the factual base that might serve the defence of such a person, whether something useful could be learned from those individuals, whether the general situation could be assessed based on the statement. When I say "the general situation," I mean the situation amongst the enemy. Those reports were then read by brigade commanders - there were several of them during my tour of duty - and also the chief of the security organ would read those reports, and they would jointly make a decision on how to use the facts that I had gathered. So this concerned my job. This was part of my duties. This was part of the description of my job, and this is where my role finished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to take you step by step. First of all, you indicated that at some point your function was to question people to see whether they had -- were involved in any incidents, whether they were serious or non-serious. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please tell us, first of all, who would determine who you would be questioning? Who would determine that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: It was my duty to hear any person that had been brought in by the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: And the actual decision to that effect was brought by whoever -- whosoever was issuing orders in the military police. The basic decision as to whether that person would be brought before me was actually brought by the person in charge in the military police, so I could not interrogate anyone on my own initiative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Were you in your capacity - and it sounds as if you were sort of like a lawyer in the brigade - in your capacity, were you able to conduct investigations?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was not some sort of a lawyer; I was a lawyer. I could not conduct investigations. I could only take statements from people brought before me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what would happen with those statements?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I had to and was duty-bound to take those statements to the commander for him to decide what is to be done with the persons who had breached either discipline or a law or what have you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's start with the discipline. Are those serious or non-serious offenses?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: These were lesser offenses, less-grave offenses. I can give you an example, if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, give us an example.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: For instance, AWOL soldiers, who leave the unit without leave and then stay at home for a couple of days without authorisation by their superior commander, then the commander in question would inform the military police of that particular incident, the military police would bring the person in, I would take the statement from the person thus brought in, and I would inform the commander that one or two persons or more persons, as the case may be, have given a statement and that this is a breach of discipline punishable by military detention in military prison. If the consequences are of minor nature, of course the offence can be pardoned. If the commander decides that the person should be punished by any kind of sanction, it was up to him to tell me, here, you draw up a text of an order with all the necessary reasoning and explanation as a jurist and bring it to me to sign. So I would do that. I would transact the technical part of the job, and I would, of course, take that order to the commander for his signature and authentication, as he was the only person who was empowered to sign an order punishing a soldier. After that, the military police would receive, either directly from the commander or from the organ in charge, this order and would then bring the person in question to military detention, which was a facility which existed there and could accommodate a number of persons. And that is as far as that part of that particular assignment is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What if the offence was something much more serious than disciplinary action? A criminal offence. How would that be handled? What would you do?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, procedurally speaking, the same thing. However, another consideration, or rather, another legal obligation had to be observed in this particular instance; namely, the commander could not take a decision and impose a penalty for a criminal offence, because that is in the jurisdiction of courts, specifically in the case of the military court which was in charge of our area. So I would observe, follow the same procedure: I would inform the commander what criminal offence was in question, I would prepare what documentation I could, and such a person, in case of the gravest criminal offenses, for instance, grievous bodily harm or murder, would be then referred, with the aid of the police, to the investigating magistrate of the military court which used to be in Sokolac and later in Bijeljina when the territorial jurisdiction changed, in order for him to institute proceedings in keeping with the criminal code -- the criminal procedure code. There would be an accompanying letter with a person and, in addition to it, usually a criminal report, a criminal information to be laid to the criminal military investigator would also be made in order for action to be taken against such a perpetrator or a violator, rather, of the law -- or a perpetrator of a criminal offence. Then the court would proceed as envisaged under the criminal procedure law; first of all the investigation and then the actual trial until the final resolution of the case, which was by then a totally legal matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to please slow down a little bit. Let me guide you through this process.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's all right. Now, once the matter is referred to the military prosecutor and then it goes up to the military investigative Judge, at that phase would you be involved at all in assisting?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Very little. Only in one sense. If the investigating Judge of the military court decided - and he could under the law - to conduct certain investigative actions outside the seat of the court in the specific instance in the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade, in some of the rooms, he could do so. He could have a room made available and a secretary, perhaps, for his benefit to conduct it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Other than providing those facilities, would you be engaged in any other activities?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not in those processes, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we get to the events surrounding Srebrenica, while you were with the Bratunac Brigade, were you ever a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was, at the very beginning of the war. Because I was mobilised into that particular unit. That was from the 16th of April. I can't recall dates with precision, but my son was born on that date, that is why I remember it. So -- that was until the end of April when I was demobilised, and then again from the 1st of June or the 1st of July, I'm not quite sure, I was mobilised again into the military police. But I was immediately assigned to this particular duty. I did no regular military police duty like patrols and things that are the normal routine of military police. So the emphasis was on technical and legal affairs, which I had to conduct, as I explained a while ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And during that period and thereafter, did you take -- did you have an opportunity to take statements from individuals pursuant to your functions?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just for the record, let me show you what has been marked for identification as D167. If you could take a look at it. Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I recognise what it is, but I myself have not seen it so far. I know what its content is; it is a report on the strength of the numbers of the force in the military police, signed by the commander Milos Petrovic. And inter alia, it contains my name on the very end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me walk you through. What is the date on this document?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: The 24th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to the last page, because you indicated your name is there. Right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the content in this document accurate?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, relatively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me show you another document which has been marked as D168. If you could look at this document. Just look at it, please. Let me walk you through it step by step.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a report on military duties and work in the military police, as it was dubbed. I compiled the report; this is my name and this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me remind you, I would like to go through these documents step by step. First of all, what is the date on this document? I'm referring to D168. What's the date on it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: The 4th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And as you noted, your name appears in the last page. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No dilemma about that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No dilemma.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please tell us, what is this document about?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: This document is a report on military duties and work from the very outbreak of the war until the date when it was compiled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was this report made, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I do recall. It was compiled at the request of the head of the organ for OB affairs, intelligence affairs. He asked that the report be compiled, and probably also the commander of the brigade. I'm not quite sure of that particular fact, but most probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And who prepared this document, since it bears your name on it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this document it refers to you having interrogated some prisoners, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, on page 3 in the English version, it notes that there were 35 prisoners, to be exact. Correct? In the English version it's -- it would be page 2 in your version. If you go one, two, three, the fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you please tell us: What was the purpose of interrogating these captured soldiers and other persons that you, over here, designate as Muslims and as prisoners of war? What was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose was to identify the captured persons and to gather from them data as terms of where they had come from, what was the situation in terms of the enemy's weapons, the enemy's morale, where the combat positions of the enemy were, and most importantly, to try to find out what the intentions of the enemy were, given the fact that in those months many Serbian villages had been attacked and burnt down. So the emphasis was on trying to get intelligence as to when was the enemy planning to attack our positions or what places he was planning to attack; what village, what town, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please tell us, to your knowledge and to your understanding, what happened to the 35 prisoners of war that you were involved in interrogating? And this would have been sometime between April 1992 and March 1993, in that period.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: After I'd taken statements from these persons, from such persons, these persons would be then escorted to detention, the detention facility. And this was seen to by the commander of the brigade -- actually, in that particular period we had first the garrison commander and then the brigade was formed only later. So terminologically speaking, it was always the commander of whatever level of unit was concerned. And as far as I know, some of those persons were sent to be -- to Batkovic to be exchanged, Batkovic near Bijeljina. Whether it was a collection centre, a detention centre, a prison, it was one of those things. And some of these persons from whom I had taken statements were entrusted to me to take them to Potocari and to hand them over to the armed forces in Srebrenica, which I certainly did. So I handed them over there to them in their territory, and some of -- in regard of some of those persons, the brigade commander tasked me with reporting them to the International Red Cross or the UNHCR - I cannot remember exactly at this point - and to hand them over to them. This was four or five elderly people whom we fed and took care of until the moment when I handed them over to these organisations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In light --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I have -- I had a few papers on this handing and take-over with the representatives of the Red Cross. That is it. That is all that I know about the further fate of these people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me ask you: In light of your position, why were you involved in making these arrangements or having contact with the Red Cross and exchanging -- or delivering, I should say, prisoners of war to the UNHCR or to the other side? Why you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: In my reply, I would proceed from an explanation. I cannot reply with a simple yes or no. If you would allow me, I would like to amplify a bit. For the simple reason that I was a person that had not been discredited in any way prior to the outbreak of the conflict, so I could go to the Muslim's territory, negotiate, if that was the task; to hand over prisoners, if that was my task. So these very same persons that I took statements from, I would escort myself and hand them over to their people in their territory. They perhaps should have also added to the description of my job also the desk officer for humanitarian affairs, but it was somehow implied, in addition to my regular duties, I would also be performing tasks of this nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in this report you compiled for your superior officer, as far as what you had been engaged in, it also appears that you were doing some intelligence and even counter-intelligence work. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we then see the name of Lieutenant Drago Nikolic. Is that the same Drago Nikolic who ultimately ends up in the Zvornik Brigade, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I know just this one Drago Nikolic. It was, I believe, August, and until the end of September 1992 this person was in contact with me and never again afterwards. But I believe that at the time he was at Sekovici. Now, whether he went to Zvornik later, I'm not sure. I believe that this is that Dragan, or rather, Drago person. There is no other that I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please explain to us a little bit, sir, so at least we have a sense of your duties, what exactly do you -- were you doing with respect to intelligence and counter-intelligence work? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, frankly speaking, the terms used here are "intelligence" and "counter-intelligence." I really don't know much about those things, about those affairs, but I will tell you what to my mind were intelligence and counter-intelligence affairs. Intelligence work was gathering all possible information about the situation of the enemy on the basis of statements taken or on the basis of some other sources of information in order to portray a picture about the intentions of the enemy, whether he means to attack or burn down a village or not. And similar things in this context; what armaments he had at disposal, where he had his fortified lines and placements from where he could attack us. This is what I understand to be intelligence. And counter-intelligence was, in a way, drawing, my drawing of conclusions, which I would then present to this Mr. Drago Nikolic as to what the situation was, seeing that I was in charge of morale as the desk officer, what was the situation in that particular respect among the troops; whether they were deserting, whether they had complaints, and similar. And possibly whether there was an information from our soldiers or from civilians of collaboration with the enemy, or of our soldiers or civilians collaborating with the enemy, which we simply call treason. So that was the kind of information I was looking for. I didn't gather much of such counter-intelligence information. As for intelligence gathering, that was a standard, and I have already described it: Where it was, which unit, how well armed it was, and things of that character. Later we had a chief of intelligence and security appointed, and after he had been appointed, I believe it was in October or November 1992, I'm not quite sure, he was thereafter in charge of this business, so I would be just there as an auxiliary staff member. And I did it because of the very chaotic situation that came at the beginning of the war, which in fact reigned on both sides, so that is why I had to do it. I hope I have managed to respond to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you have indeed, and it has been quite comprehensive, might I add. Now, I'm going to ask you to sort of keep your answers as narrow as possible and let me guide you through the process. First of all, who would you report to in your position? In light of your position, who was your commanding officer, your immediate commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Always the commander. And before the commander, not throughout the period of my service in the army, but when he was appointed the assistant commander for the same work, but he was the assistant commander and thereby he was a commanding officer, and that was Major Ratko Jevtic. And I cannot recall with precision the exact date of his appointment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But I want to focus your attention now on July 1995. In light of your position, who was your immediate commander, the one that you would report to?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: The commander was Vidoje Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just -- I think you've answered the question. I don't want to cut you off, but I want to focus you on the questions. Now, to what extent -- first of all, where were your offices?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: My offices. Not offices, I apologise; the one and only office which I had was in an auxiliary building located before you enter the yard, the compound, of the headquarters of the brigade, to the right, namely in the facility where the military police platoon was, the makeshift or auxiliary storehouse of the military police was, and my office was also there. And that is the compound of the ceramic tile factory which was called Ukrasna keramika, or decorative ceramics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not have an office in the headquarters itself where the brigade command was located?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an association with or were you ever subordinated to Momir Nikolic, who was the head of security and intelligence, in light of his position and his association with the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Momir Nikolic was never my superior commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not have to report to him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any work with him? Did you ever have any work where you would have to collaborate with; associate with; coordinate, for lack of a better term, with?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in what instances would that be?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in instances when we controlled -- for instance, we checked out UNPROFOR convoys. If Momir couldn't do it, I would do it. In other occasions if they were in a dilemma, the military police, or he himself, as to the manner of application on the law on the army, the law -- the application of force, of coercion against the soldiers, then we had consultative talks. Simply they sought my advice and I would give them my advice on these subject matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In light of your position, would you sit in on the daily briefings, if there were such, with the other brigade commanders?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I couldn't attend such briefings because I was not a member of the command. I'm not an officer. I was a foot soldier. Nobody invited me to any such briefings. It was not my duty to go and attend such meetings, save for some exceptional cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to give you two days that we're going to use as reference points, and we'll take it from there. The first date is July 6th, 1995, and that's when the events surrounding Srebrenica commenced. And then July 11th, which we know as a fixed date for when Srebrenica fell. Now, my first question is: Prior to the events concerning Srebrenica, that is prior to July 6th, 1995, were you given any particular tasks concerning those events, the events that would ensue relating to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would you please tell us whether you were on duty at the time.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. On that day or generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, were you on vacation, general leave, or were you sick, or were you on duty?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I think, as the witness indicated, it's a little unclear what the time frame is, and "generally speaking" doesn't seem to assist us in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the answer is I can understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe the time frame is from the 6th of July to the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If we go further -- if we go to the question, which is rather clear: "Prior to July 6th, were you given any particular tasks?" The answer is: "No." "All right. Would you please tell us whether you were on duty at that time." And he says he didn't understand the question. I'll rephrase it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At or around July 6th, were you on duty or were you on leave?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm really not very good with dates. However, if I am to remember, I was never on leave. I was always on duty. I was performing my regular duties. During that period of time, I wasn't given any tasks on top of my everyday duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, during -- from the 6th to the 11th of July, that is from the time when the events concerning Srebrenica began to the time when Srebrenica fell, were you asked to go to the front, to any of the lines?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Pribicevac, for instance, where the Drina Corps had set up its forward command post and where the 3rd Battalion had its regular command post?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given any instructions, any orders, any suggestions by your commander, Colonel Blagojevic, for that period, that is from July 6th to July 11th?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether Colonel Blagojevic came to visit you during that period, from July 6th to July 11th, where you had your offices in the annex which is in front of the command post where the military police are also generally housed?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, on July 11th, we know for a fact that that was the date that Srebrenica fell. Could you please tell us if you recall that particular date. Does that date stand out, being that it was, at least for some, a rather memorable occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I must repeat for the Chamber, I'm really not very good with dates. I remember events, but I'm not so good with dates. I can't tell with precision that I remember the 11th of July, 1995. I do remember the event, however, because the events is what sticks in my mind much better than the dates. I apologise in advance for not being sure about the dates. I don't want this Trial Chamber to draw a wrong conclusion about the things that I'm saying here. I'm here to tell the truth and only the truth the way I remember it, according to the solemn declaration that I read out. Please forgive me for not remembering the precise dates, for not being precise. As for the events that took place, I can describe the events as much as I remember them and to the extent I participated in those events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Celanovic, let's talk about events then. All right.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, do you recall the day -- forget about the date, but do you recall the event, the date, when Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I cannot be too precise about that either. I know what in my mind was the thing that marked the fall of Srebrenica. And I don't know whether this was on that particular date. To my mind, Srebrenica fell when it became clear -- when you say "Srebrenica," I understand the whole enclave, not just the town of Srebrenica. To my mind, it was on the 13th when the majority of the detainees came to Bratunac. I did hear, however, that it fell on the 11th or on the 12th. I can tell you about the events the way I experienced them, and then you pinpoint a date. I don't want to be -- to make a mistake about things only because I don't remember the dates of things that happened such a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Mr. Celanovic, let's stick to events then. Do you recall sometime during that period, that is after the 11th -- after Srebrenica fell, do you recall whether you questioned -- you were asked to question any prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I remember that very clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Good. Now, we're going to go step by step. Do you recall -- well, I'll take a shot at it: Do you recall what day it was that you were asked to do that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, I can't be sure whether it was on the 12th or on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall where you were when you were asked to question any prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I was in front of the building where my office was, in the yard in front of that building, to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall the time of day? Was it morning or evening or afternoon or around lunchtime?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that for a fact, but I would say that it was morning, in the morning of the day when most of the detainees arrived and when I interrogated some of them, when I took their statements. Before I took their statements, I had to identify them, I had to take their particulars for identification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We're going to go step by step. Just work with me here. First of all, who was it that asked you to question the POWs, since you've told us earlier that you normally did not do investigations but you would question at request once requested? So who was it that ordered you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Ljubisa Beara ordered it. I believe that he was a colonel by rank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you know Mr. Beara from before?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met him on several occasions when he came for inspections to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you know -- do you know where Mr. Beara fit in to the structure in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that he was an officer for intelligence and security with the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army. That's what I thought at the time. He was either in charge of the intelligence and security or maybe some other service with the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, could you please tell us what exactly Colonel Beara told you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN CELANOVIC
utterances.text: He found me in front of the building, and he asked me what I was doing, whether I was just wasting my time - I was standing outside, it was very hot - or whether I was busy doing something. I told him that I was busy doing my job, and as he knew that I had started gathering information on crimes committed against the Serbian population, I had started gathering statements from the Serbian population that had survived massacres and killings of members of their family, I told him that I already had some statements, and I told him that he would find it best systematised in The Chronicle of Our Graveyards, the author of which was Milivoje Ivanisevic. When I look at this information, although this book is also not perfect, when it comes to data, I can find things out. He told me in case it happened that they brought somebody in or in case somebody ordered for somebody to be brought in, either the army or the police - and when he said "somebody," he was referring to Muslims - that I should try and inspect their IDs to see who these people are and to find out whether any of those could be found in that book, in the list. And when I say "the list," I'm referring to the book Chronicle of Our Graveyards by Milivoje Ivanisevic. This was very much the method of a random sample. If somebody was brought in, we should try and identify the person. And if that name could be found in the book, then I should try and inform one of the officers of the security services, with a view to sending this person to the district court in Bijeljina for further proceedings, because the names in the book were the names of the suspects who probably committed crimes against the civilian population in the area. This is what he told me to do, to take the particulars of the persons who were brought in, to establish their identity if one way or another. One way was to see whether anybody knew the person who was brought in, if they didn't have any ID on them. And this is exactly what I did with the persons who were brought in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. Now, I believe it's time -- that's all we have for today, though I will ask you to please listen to my questions and let me guide you through tomorrow so we can do this step by step, but I appreciate your complete answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Witness, I'm afraid you have to stay in The Hague for another day because we did not finish your testimony. And during your stay here, you are still under oath, so do not talk to anybody and do not let anybody talk to you about your testimony. And the hearing is adjourned for today, and we'll meet tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: at 1.47 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 19th day of May, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
